pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of the house in this workspace. Share it with editors, production, rights and the person who runs royalties.
: who we publish, their agent, advances, and royalties due and paid.
: the submissions pile with readers and respond-by dates.
: each book through its editorial stages, with ISBN, page count, advance, list price, royalty rate, copies sold, royalties earned and what is still unearned.
: edits, design, proofs, index and metadata, with freelancers.
: each printing, the copies, the cost and when books arrive.
: audio, translation, film, large print and book club.
: twice a year for every author.
Monday: the dashboard. Steps due, books arriving, answers owed to agents.
Tuesday: production meeting on every title publishing in the next six months.
Twice a year: royalty statement season.
Every morning: production steps due and blocked
Every week: manuscripts answered on time, print runs confirmed
Every season: metadata out four months ahead
Every half year: statements prepared, checked and paid

Acquiring editors own manuscripts and their titles' editorial stages. The managing editor owns the production calendar. Production owns print runs and printers. The rights manager owns rights. Finance owns royalty statements. The publisher reads the whole list.

text.text: A book takes nine to eighteen months from signed contract to publication day. The dates work backwards from publication, and every one of them is in this workspace.

: cover and interior. Cover approval needs the editor, sales and the author.
: a proofreader and the author read typeset pages. Changes now are costly; fix errors, not sentences.

The ISBN, page count, price and description go to distributors at least four months before publication. Late metadata means fewer pre-orders.
Steps overdue or blocked, with a plan for each
Print runs on order: files sent on time, delivery dates confirmed
Metadata sent for every title publishing in the next four months

Moss and the Moon is a picture book publishing soon, but its cover is blocked while the illustrator revises the moon. The managing editor moved the interior layout forward so the designer is not idle, confirmed a color print slot with Lakeside, and told sales the cover would be final within a week.

Authors judge a publisher by two things: how their book was treated and whether their statements are right and on time. Statements go out twice a year, for the first half and second half of the year, usually within three months of the period ending.
as a percentage of list price, set in the contract. Common rates are 10 percent for hardcovers, 7.5 percent for paperbacks and 5 percent each to author and illustrator on picture books.
is what the distributor reports, less books stores sent back.
is copies times list price times the rate.
The advance is paid against royalties. Until it is earned out, statements show a balance but no payment.
Rights income, such as audio or translation, is shared with the author at the split in the contract, usually half.
Download the distributor's sales and returns report for the period.
for every author with a title on sale, even if nothing is owed. Authors want to know.
Hold a reserve against returns on new titles, usually 15 to 20 percent of the period's sales, and release it over the next two statements.
A second person checks every statement before it moves to
. Send the statement with a short note from the editor; a line about how the book is doing goes a long way.

and answer within two weeks with the distributor's numbers. Most queries are about returns or rights income timing.

A Small History of Harbors sold 4,180 copies net at $29 and 10 percent, earning about $12,100 against a $7,500 advance. It has earned out, so Cornelius Adebayo's statement shows a payment, plus half the German translation fee.
Every book on the list started as a manuscript in the pile. A fair, quick process means agents send their best work to us first.
Every manuscript that arrives goes into
the day it lands, with the author, the agent, the genre, the word count and a
date. Agented submissions get an answer within four to six weeks; unagented within three months. If you will be late, tell the agent before the date, not after.
The reader reads the first fifty pages and the synopsis. Three outcomes:
: another editor reads the whole manuscript.
Every manuscript past a first read gets a one-page report: what it is in two sentences, what works, what does not, two or three comparable recent titles and how they sold, and a recommendation.

The editor makes the case in five minutes.
Sales gives a realistic first-year estimate.
The publisher sets the offer: advance, royalty rates, territory, formats and the rights we want.
